edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), Arnobius, Disputationes adversus gentes, Liber I, via Latin Wikisource (Corpus Corporum TEI)
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Quae sunt ista, inquies, clausa atque obscura mysteria, quae nulli nec homines scire, nec ipsi, qui appellantur, dii mundi, parte queunt aliqua suspicionis atque opinationis attingere, nisi quos ipse dignatus est cognitionis tantae impertire muneribus, et in abditos recessus thesauri interioris inducere. Vides enim, si nollet inferri sibi a quoquam manus, summa illi fuisse contentione nitendum, ut hostes ab se suos, vel potestate inversa prohiberet? Qui caecis restituerat lumina, is efficere si deberet, non poterat caecos? qui debilibus integritatem, is debiles reddere difficultati habuit, aut labori? qui claudos faciebat incedere, is motus alligare membrorum nervorum duritia nesciebat? qui extrahebat a tumulis mortuos, huic arduum fuerat letum cui vellet indicere? Sed quia fieri ratio ea, quae fuerant destinata, poscebat: et hic in ipso mundo, nec modo quam gestum est alio, inaestimabilis illa atque incredibilis lenitas injurias in se hominum, puerilibus pro ineptiis ducens, manus in se porrigi ab immanibus passa est, durissimisque latronibus, nec reputandum putavit, quid illorum dissignasset audacia, dummodo suis ostenderet, quid ab sese expectare deberent. Cum enim de animarum periculis multa, mala de illarum contra insinuator, magister atque auctor, ad officiorum convenientium fines, suas leges et constituta direxit: non superbiae factum comminuit? non libidinum extinxit flammas? non hiatum compressit aviditatis? non tela extorsit e manibus, atque omnia seminaria totius vitiositatis abscidit? Ipse denique non lenis, non placidus, non accessu facilis, non familiaris affatu, non humanas miserias indolescens, omnes omnino crucibus et corporalibus affectos malis unica illa benignitate miseratus, reddidit et restituit sanitati?
pass_a_gloss: What are these, you will say, closed and obscure mysteries, which neither men nor the gods of the world can know, nor can they even touch with any suspicion or opinion, except those to whom He Himself has deigned to impart the gifts of such great knowledge and to lead into the hidden recesses of the inner treasure. For you see, if He did not want anyone to lay hands on Him, He would have had to strive with the greatest effort to prevent His enemies from doing so, or to prevent them by reversed power. He who restored sight to the blind, could He not make the blind if He had to? He who gave integrity to the weak, did He have difficulty in making the weak or in causing labor? He who made the lame walk, did He not know how to bind the movements of the limbs with hardness? He who raised the dead from their tombs, would it have been hard for Him to indicate death to whom He wished? But because reason demanded that what had been destined should happen, and He in this very world, not only as it was done elsewhere, endured that incredible and inestimable leniency, injuries from men, considering them childish foolishness, and allowed hands to be laid on Him by savage men and very harsh robbers, and did not think it worth considering what audacity they had assigned to themselves, as long as He showed His own what they ought to expect from Him. For when He, the insinuator, teacher, and author of the dangers of souls, directed His laws and established rules for the limits of suitable duties, did He not diminish the deed of pride? did He not extinguish the flames of lust? did He not compress the void of greed? did He not wrench the weapons from their hands and cut off all the seedbeds of total vice? He Himself, finally, not gentle, not placid, not easily accessible, not familiar in conversation, not unaware of human miseries, pitied all those afflicted with crosses and bodily evils with that unique benignity, and restored them to health?

choices.why: preserves the original phrase's emphasis on the magnitude of God's leniency

choices.english: all those afflicted with crosses and bodily evils
choices.term: omnes omnino crucibus et corporalibus affectos malis
choices.why: accurate translation of the phrase, including the scope of God's pity

pass_b_english: You will ask what these closed, obscure mysteries are that neither human beings nor the so-called gods of the world can know, nor even touch with any suspicion or opinion—except those to whom He Himself has deigned to impart the gifts of such great knowledge and to lead into the hidden recesses of the inner treasure.

Consider: if He had not wanted anyone to lay hands on Him, He would have had to strive with the utmost effort to keep His enemies away, or else He could have prevented them by a simple reversal of power.

He who restored sight to the blind—could He not have made them blind if He had chosen to? He who gave integrity to the weak—did He find it difficult to make them weak or to bring them labor? He who made the lame walk—did He not know how to bind the movements of their limbs with hardness? He who raised the dead from their tombs—would it have been hard for Him to decree death for whomever He wished?

But reason demanded that what had been destined should happen, and so in this very world—not merely as it was done elsewhere—He endured that incredible, inestimable leniency, suffering the injuries of men and treating them as childish foolishness.

He allowed savage men and very harsh robbers to lay hands on Him, and He did not think it worth considering what audacity they had assigned to themselves, provided He showed His own what they ought to expect from Him.

For when He, the insinuator, teacher, and author of the dangers of souls, directed His laws and established rules to the limits of suitable duties, did He not diminish the deed of pride? Did He not extinguish the flames of lust? Did He not compress the void of greed? Did He not wrench the weapons from their hands and cut off all the seedbeds of total vice?

Finally, He Himself—not gentle, not placid, not easily accessible, not familiar in conversation, not unaware of human miseries—pitied all those afflicted with crosses and bodily evils with that unique benignity, and restored them to health.
